props.title: Rosemary's Baby

sections.content: Rosemary's Baby revolutionized psychological horror by bringing satanic terror into an upscale Manhattan apartment building. Roman Polanski's masterpiece of paranoid horror crafted a new template for domestic terror that influenced films like The Exorcist (1973) and The Omen (1976). Mia Farrow's haunting performance as Rosemary Woodhouse captures the mounting dread of a woman whose pregnancy becomes a nightmare, while Ruth Gordon's seemingly friendly neighbor Minnie Castevet masks sinister intentions behind her nosy charm. The film's genius lies in making the everyday terrifying - prenatal vitamins, apartment neighbors, and even a husband's career ambitions become weapons of psychological torture.

sections.content: The film's urban setting marked a crucial shift from Gothic horror's remote castles to modern apartments. This claustrophobic domesticity influenced later works like The Shining (1980) and Repulsion (1965), where familiar spaces become traps. The Dakota building itself becomes a character, its ornate architecture and dark corridors reflecting the decay beneath civilized society. This approach to location-as-character would later influence films like The Devil's Advocate (1997) and Hereditary (2018), where upscale homes harbor ancient evils.

Polanski's masterful direction creates uncertainty through subtle details rather than overt scares. The gaslighting of Rosemary by her husband Guy and the Castevets established a template for psychological manipulation that influenced films like Get Out (2017) and Mother! (2017). The film's exploration of bodily autonomy and medical gaslighting remains frighteningly relevant, seen in modern horror like Saint Maud (2020) and False Positive (2021). sections.content: The film's impact on contemporary horror cannot be overstated. Midsommar (2019) and The Witch (2015) follow its template of daylight horror and insidious cults masquerading as community. The theme of pregnancy horror influenced Inside (2007) and The Babadook (2014), while its exploration of urban isolation can be seen in Under the Shadow (2016) and Raw (2016).
